problem: The sentence 'Two-stroke does not mean two strokes per cycle in the four-stroke sense' is confusing and partly false: a two-stroke cycle does consist of exactly two strokes (one up, one down). The real point is that each stroke does two jobs, and the wording as written can leave a student thinking a two-stroke cycle has some other number of strokes.
fix: A two-stroke cycle has only two strokes — one up and one down — so each stroke does two jobs: the down stroke is power plus scavenging, the up stroke is compression plus crankcase intake. The name hides this doubling of work, not an absence of strokes.

problem: The answer says a two-stroke 'fires twice as often per revolution'. A two-stroke fires once per revolution and a four-stroke once per two revolutions; the doubling is per unit time at the same speed, not per revolution.
fix: A two-stroke fires twice as often at the same engine speed: once per revolution against once every two revolutions for a four-stroke. So it rejects more heat per second from the same cylinder and needs stronger cooling, which in small sizes is air cooling with fins; a four-stroke of the same size rejects less heat per second and is easier to cool, and car four-strokes use liquid cooling.
